rationale: The evidence documents only Bland's own MCP server, which lets external coding agents control a Bland account. That is the server role and says nothing about Bland voice agents consuming MCP servers as tool sources. Mid-call tools are shown only as custom HTTP API integrations and webhooks, with no evidence that a voice agent can plug in an MCP server to gain whole toolsets.

Bland documents an official MCP server that lets coding agents manage agents, build and validate pathways, and place calls. It also has an official CLI to make calls, build pathways and configure phone numbers, plus a Pathways API and an agent-driven signup flow over plain API calls, so the create-agent, attach-number and place-call chain can be done without the dashboard. Missing for 10: no single documented end-to-end provisioning walkthrough explicitly covering number purchase or attachment through MCP or API, no published OpenAPI spec (probes returned 404), and no independent or hands-on corroboration.

A live probe confirms https://docs.bland.ai/llms.txt returns HTTP 200 with a Bland documentation index. The docs are served as raw .md pages, and there are explicitly agent-oriented resources: a 'connect your agent' flow written for bots, an MCP server that can search the Bland docs, and a recommended coding-agent plugin. Missing for 10: independent or hands-on corroboration that an agent pointed at these docs works well, and no evidence of an llms-full.txt or similar full-content export.

Bland's in-product Evals use LLM judges to grade each dimension of your calls, which is a form of AI-generated assessment of your own call data. There is no evidence of AI-generated insights, summaries, or improvement suggestions surfaced in the product. Analytics querying is documented only through the external MCP server driven by a coding agent, not inside the product. Missing for 10: in-product AI insights or summaries across call data, AI-generated suggestions or recommendations, independent or hands-on corroboration.

Bland documents triggers that watch for events and act on them, such as calling a customer when a support case is created. It also supports batch call campaigns from a CSV and post-call webhooks it sends automatically. Together these let event-driven automations run without a human in the loop. missing for 10: details on trigger sources and configuration (only a one-line description), any scheduled or recurring automation capability, and independent or hands-on confirmation that background automations work reliably.

The evidence describes no built-in AI assistant inside the Bland product that users can hand tasks to. The MCP server, CLI and plugin let external coding agents operate a Bland account, and the voice agents and LLM eval judges are what customers build or configure. None of these is an in-product assistant that takes delegated tasks.

Bland can be driven without its UI. An official CLI manages the whole account from the terminal, including making calls and building and testing pathways (bland-docs-12, bland-probe-4). Pathways can also be created programmatically via API (bland-docs-1), and batch calls, post-call webhooks and triggers support automated flows (bland-docs-6, bland-docs-5, bland-docs-41). missing for 10: explicit CI/CD pipeline integration docs or examples, documented non-interactive auth for CI runners, a published OpenAPI spec (probe found none), and independent hands-on corroboration of headless or CI use.

The evidence shows only Bland's own MCP server, which lets external coding agents control a Bland account (a server-side role), and generic HTTP API integrations. Nothing shows Bland agents connecting to external MCP servers as tool sources.

Bland's first-party docs describe an official MCP server that lets AI agents place and inspect calls, send texts, build and validate pathways, manage agents, query analytics, run evals and search the docs. Missing for 10: independent or hands-on corroboration that connecting an agent through the MCP server works in practice.

Missing for 10: a native in-product natural-language command interface (natural-language operation is only shown through external AI agents), and independent hands-on corroboration that the natural-language operations work as described.
